South Korea's National Pension Service (NPS) has appointed Lee Kyu-hong, former head of fund management at the Teachers' Pension, as its new chief…

Lee Kyu-hong, former head of the fund management division at the Teachers' Pension (TP), has been selected as the new investment chief of South Korea's National Pension Service (NPS), which manages ₩1,866 trillion (approximately $1.4 trillion) in retirement savings for South Korean citizens. A "pension fund purist" who has worked across private asset managers, real estate investment firms, and public pension funds, Lee now takes the helm as CIO of one of the world's largest pension funds.

The NPS announced on the 14th that it had appointed Lee as its new fund management director. He assumes office on the 15th, with a two-year term running through September 14, 2028. The position may be renewed on a one-year basis depending on job performance. The fund management director is appointed by the NPS chairman following a recommendation from the Fund Management Director Recommendation Committee and approval of a performance contract by South Korea's Minister of Health and Welfare.

The selection process was reportedly delayed for an extended period at the final consultation stage, despite the personnel vetting report having been submitted to the presidential office earlier this month. Unlike the usual practice of narrowing the final candidate pool to two or three individuals, this time four candidates advanced to the vetting stage—a development industry observers described as unusual.

The final candidates included Park Cheon-seok, former head of fund management at MG Community Credit Cooperatives; Lee Do-yoon, former head of asset management at the Yellow Umbrella Mutual Aid Fund; and Kim Ho-jin, former head of fund management at the National Federation of Fisheries Cooperatives. After a four-way race that continued until the final stage, Lee—who has accumulated experience in both private asset management and public pension funds—ultimately secured the appointment.

Born in 1966, Lee graduated from Yonsei University's business school and earned an MBA from New York University's Stern School of Business. He began his career in the research team at Samsung Asset Management, followed by stints as a research analyst at SG Securities, in the research and analysis team at DB Asset Management, and in the asset management division at Eastspring Asset Management.

From 2013 to 2018, he served as CIO of NH-Amundi Asset Management. He then became CEO of Ascendas Asset Management, a real estate-focused investment firm, before serving as CIO of the Teachers' Pension from 2019 to 2023. Since 2024, he has worked as an advisor in the corporate finance division at the law firm Shin & Kim.

Lee is regarded as a "multi-asset" investment specialist with experience spanning traditional assets and alternative investments. Analysts note that his extensive experience managing overseas assets—more than any other candidate—was a decisive factor in his final selection. His four years overseeing fund management at the Teachers' Pension as CIO is also cited as a key strength.

His performance during his tenure at the Teachers' Pension is noteworthy. The fund posted returns of 11.15% in 2019, 11.49% in 2020, and 11.95% in 2021—three consecutive years in the 11% range. In 2021, the fund generated ₩2.4738 trillion (approximately $1.8 billion) in investment income, the largest in the institution's history. Completing his initial two-year term and then securing two consecutive renewals was also considered exceptional.

The biggest challenge facing the new CIO is sustaining long-term returns while stably managing a rapidly growing fund. NPS reserves reached ₩1,866 trillion at the end of June. First-half investment returns hit 27.22%, the highest half-year performance on record. Domestic equities returned 107.37% and overseas equities 17.81%, driving the strong results.

Adjusting the sharply changed asset composition is another key task. As of the end of June, the NPS held approximately ₩543 trillion (approximately $401.5 billion) in domestic equities, ₩661 trillion (approximately $488.7 billion) in overseas equities, and ₩261 trillion (approximately $193.0 billion) in alternative investments. The stock market surge pushed the domestic equity allocation to 29.1% of total financial assets.

Although the Fund Management Committee raised this year's domestic equity target allocation from 14.9% to 20.8% and widened the permissible range, the NPS must also minimize the market impact of its trading as it adjusts allocations across asset classes in response to market conditions.

Integrated risk management of an increasingly complex portfolio—alongside the expansion of overseas and alternative investments—is also cited as a critical priority. As the fund grows larger, the allocation ratios across domestic and overseas equities, bonds, and alternative assets, and how these are adjusted according to market phases, have a greater impact on overall performance than achieving high returns on individual investments.

Lee also faces the task of strengthening internal controls within the investment organization and restoring trust. The NPS has recently been investigating allegations of leaked non-public investment information involving its real estate investment division, while also conducting information security and confidentiality training for all employees as part of broader internal control reinforcement.

A senior investment banking industry official said, "As the fund grows larger, asset allocation capability—coordinating the entire portfolio—becomes more important than performance in any specific asset class." The official added, "How the new director, who has served as CIO at both a private asset manager and a public pension fund, reshapes a portfolio approaching ₩1,900 trillion (approximately $1.4 trillion) will be the biggest point of interest for the domestic and international asset management industry."

A pension fund industry source said, "The new CIO will be expected to demonstrate not only investment performance but also leadership in stabilizing organizational management and decision-making systems."

With Lee's appointment, the tenure of Seo Won-joo, who had been serving as acting CIO since his official term ended late last year pending the selection of a successor, also comes to a close.

Separately, the NPS also appointed Kim Dae-soon as its new welfare director on the same day. Kim is an internal candidate who joined the NPS in 1999 and has served as head of strategic management, director of the future innovation planning unit, and head of the IT division.
